questions.q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.fact: Mars looks red because its dust has a lot of rusty iron in it.

questions.q: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
questions.fact: Jupiter is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.

questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.fact: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and also the smallest planet.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist who studies stars and planets?
questions.fact: Astronomers use telescopes and math to learn about stars, planets, and galaxies.

questions.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon in 1969 during the Apollo 11 mission.

questions.q: Who was the first person to travel into space?
questions.fact: Yuri Gagarin of the Soviet Union orbited Earth in 1961.

questions.q: Which planet is famous for its big, bright rings?
questions.fact: Saturn's rings are made of countless chunks of ice and rock.

questions.q: What is the name of the galaxy we live in?
questions.fact: Our solar system is one small part of the Milky Way, a galaxy with billions of stars.

questions.q: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
questions.fact: Venus has thick clouds that trap heat, so it is even hotter than Mercury.

questions.q: How long does it take Earth to travel once around the Sun?
questions.fact: Earth takes about 365 days to orbit the Sun. That trip is what we call a year.

questions.q: What causes day and night on Earth?
questions.fact: Earth spins once about every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day.

questions.q: What is a shooting star really?
questions.fact: A shooting star is a meteor, a bit of space rock that glows as it burns up in Earth's air.

questions.q: What force keeps the planets moving around the Sun?
questions.fact: The Sun's gravity pulls on the planets and keeps them in their orbits.

questions.q: Which planet spins tipped over on its side?
questions.fact: Uranus is tilted so much that it spins almost on its side as it orbits the Sun.

questions.q: What was the name of the first satellite launched into space in 1957?
questions.fact: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 in 1957, which started the space age.

questions.q: Which famous space telescope was launched into orbit in 1990?
questions.fact: The Hubble Space Telescope orbits Earth and has taken amazing pictures of faraway galaxies.

questions.q: What does a light-year measure?
questions.fact: A light-year is how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers.

questions.q: Which planet has a giant storm called the Great Red Spot?
questions.fact: The Great Red Spot is a huge storm on Jupiter that has been seen for more than 150 years.

questions.q: How many planets are in our solar system?
questions.fact: There are eight planets. In 2006, Pluto was moved into a group called dwarf planets.

questions.q: Which planet is farthest from the Sun?
questions.fact: Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun. It is cold, windy, and deep blue.

questions.q: What is the largest animal on Earth today?
questions.fact: A blue whale can grow to about 30 meters long, longer than two school buses.

questions.q: What is the fastest land animal?
questions.fact: Cheetahs can run over 100 km per hour, but only for short sprints.

questions.q: How many legs does a spider have?
questions.fact: Spiders have eight legs. Insects have six, so spiders are not insects.

questions.q: What is a baby kangaroo called?
questions.fact: A joey is born tiny and keeps growing safely inside its mother's pouch.

questions.q: What is a group of lions called?
questions.fact: A pride is a family group of lions that lives and hunts together.

questions.q: Which bird is able to fly backward?
questions.fact: Hummingbirds beat their wings so fast they can hover in place and even fly backward.

questions.q: What is the tallest animal in the world?
questions.fact: Giraffes can be over 5 meters tall, and their long necks help them reach treetop leaves.

questions.q: Which mammal can truly fly, not just glide?
questions.fact: Bats are the only mammals that can really fly. Flying squirrels can only glide.

questions.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.fact: An octopus has three hearts, and its blood is blue.

questions.q: What does a caterpillar turn into when it grows up?
questions.fact: Inside a chrysalis or cocoon, a caterpillar completely changes its body.

questions.q: What is the largest bird in the world?
questions.fact: Ostriches cannot fly, but they run very fast and lay the biggest eggs of any living bird.

questions.q: What kind of animal is a Komodo dragon?
questions.fact: The Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard. It lives on a few islands in Indonesia.

questions.q: What is a young frog that lives in water and has a tail called?
questions.fact: Tadpoles breathe with gills, then grow legs and lungs as they turn into frogs.

questions.q: What food do giant pandas mostly eat?
questions.fact: Giant pandas spend many hours every day munching on bamboo.

questions.q: What type of animal is a dolphin?
questions.fact: Dolphins breathe air through a blowhole and feed their babies milk, like other mammals.

questions.q: Which sea animal has no brain, no heart, and no bones?
questions.fact: Jellyfish have no brain, heart, or bones. Their bodies are mostly water.

questions.q: How do honeybees show other bees where to find flowers?
questions.fact: Honeybees do a waggle dance that shows other bees which way to go and how far.

questions.q: Which animal spends most of its life hanging upside down in trees?
questions.fact: Sloths move so slowly that tiny green algae can grow in their fur.

questions.q: What do you call an animal that eats only plants?
questions.fact: Herbivores like cows, deer, and rabbits eat plants. Carnivores eat meat.

questions.q: What is the largest fish in the ocean?
questions.fact: The whale shark is a gentle giant that eats tiny floating plankton.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula for water?
questions.fact: Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.q: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make food?
questions.fact: Plants take in carbon dioxide and give off oxygen, which we breathe.

questions.q: At what temperature does water freeze on the Celsius scale?
questions.fact: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, which is the same as 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

questions.q: What are the three states of matter we see in everyday life?
questions.fact: Ice, water, and steam are the same stuff in three different states.

questions.q: Which scientist came up with the theory of relativity?
questions.fact: Albert Einstein's theory of relativity changed how we understand space, time, and gravity.

questions.q: What is the hardest natural material on Earth?
questions.fact: Diamonds are made of carbon atoms packed together very tightly.

questions.q: What is the center of an atom called?
questions.fact: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, and electrons move around it.

questions.q: What do solar panels use to make electricity?
questions.fact: Solar panels turn the energy in sunlight straight into electricity.

questions.q: What color do you get by mixing blue and yellow paint?
questions.fact: Blue and yellow are primary colors in paint, and together they make green.

questions.q: Which of these materials does a magnet pull on?
questions.fact: Magnets attract iron and a few other metals, like nickel and cobalt.

questions.q: Which gas makes up most of the air we breathe?
questions.fact: About 78 percent of air is nitrogen. Only about 21 percent is oxygen.

questions.q: What is the process plants use to make food from sunlight?
questions.fact: In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Au?
questions.fact: Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold.

questions.q: Which of these travels the fastest?
questions.fact: Light is so much faster than sound that you see lightning before you hear thunder.

questions.q: Which scientist wrote the three laws of motion?
questions.fact: Isaac Newton described how forces make things move, stop, and change direction.

questions.q: Which scientist won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry?
questions.fact: Marie Curie studied radioactivity and was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

questions.q: What do we call a substance made of only one kind of atom?
questions.fact: Elements like gold, oxygen, and carbon are listed on the periodic table.

questions.q: What is the pH of pure water?
questions.fact: A pH of 7 is neutral. Lower numbers are acids and higher numbers are bases.

questions.q: What is it called when liquid water turns into vapor?
questions.fact: Puddles dry up after rain because the water evaporates into the air.

questions.q: Why can't sound travel through outer space?
choices: There is no air to carry it
questions.fact: Sound needs air, water, or something solid to travel through. Space is almost empty.

questions.q: What is the largest ocean on Earth?
questions.fact: The Pacific Ocean is so big that all of Earth's land could fit inside it.

questions.q: What is the outermost layer of Earth called?
questions.fact: The crust is the thin, rocky layer we live on. It is thinnest under the oceans.

questions.q: What is Earth's inner core mostly made of?
questions.fact: Earth's inner core is a very hot, solid ball made mostly of iron and nickel.

questions.q: What is melted rock called while it is still underground?
questions.fact: Melted rock is called magma underground and lava once it comes out of a volcano.

questions.q: What instrument records the shaking from earthquakes?
questions.fact: A seismometer measures how the ground moves during an earthquake.

questions.q: Which type of rock forms when lava or magma cools and hardens?
questions.fact: Igneous rocks, like granite and basalt, form from melted rock that cooled.

questions.q: Which layer high in the sky blocks a lot of the Sun's harmful rays?
questions.fact: The ozone layer soaks up much of the Sun's ultraviolet light, which can burn skin.

questions.q: What are the giant moving pieces of Earth's crust called?
questions.fact: Earth's crust is broken into plates that slowly move a few centimeters each year.

questions.q: What was the name of the supercontinent that formed millions of years ago?
questions.fact: About 300 million years ago, most of Earth's land was joined together as Pangaea.

questions.q: In the water cycle, what is rain or snow falling from clouds called?
questions.fact: Precipitation is any water that falls from clouds, like rain, snow, sleet, or hail.

questions.q: Which tall cloud type often brings thunderstorms?
questions.fact: Cumulonimbus clouds can tower many kilometers high and bring lightning and heavy rain.

questions.q: What do we call a scientist who studies rocks and the Earth?
questions.fact: Geologists study rocks, volcanoes, and earthquakes to learn Earth's history.

questions.q: What is a huge, slow-moving river of ice called?
questions.fact: Glaciers form when snow piles up for many years and gets squeezed into ice.

questions.q: What mainly causes the ocean tides?
questions.fact: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, making the water rise and fall. The Sun helps a little too.

questions.q: What do we call a spot where hot water and steam shoot out of the ground?
questions.fact: Old Faithful in Yellowstone National Park is one of the most famous geysers.

questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere do we live in?
questions.fact: The troposphere is the lowest layer of air, and almost all weather happens there.

questions.q: What do we call the remains of ancient living things preserved in rock?
questions.fact: Fossils of bones, shells, and footprints help scientists learn about life long ago.

questions.q: Which is the coldest continent on Earth?
questions.fact: Antarctica is covered by a huge sheet of ice and is the coldest place on Earth.

questions.q: What is a hurricane called in the western Pacific Ocean?
questions.fact: Hurricanes, typhoons, and cyclones are the same kind of storm with different names by region.

questions.q: Which two things are needed to make a rainbow?
questions.fact: Raindrops bend sunlight and split it into its colors, making a rainbow.

questions.q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.fact: Your skin covers your whole body and protects you from germs, heat, and cold.

questions.q: How many bones does an adult human have?
questions.fact: Babies are born with more bones, but some of them join together as they grow.

questions.q: Which organ pumps blood around your body?
questions.fact: Your heart is a strong muscle that beats about 100,000 times a day.

questions.q: Where in your body is the smallest bone found?
questions.fact: The stapes, a tiny bone in your middle ear, is about the size of a grain of rice.

questions.q: What is the longest bone in the human body?
questions.fact: The thigh bone, called the femur, is the longest and strongest bone in your body.

questions.q: Which gas do your lungs take from the air for your body to use?
questions.fact: Your blood carries oxygen from your lungs to every part of your body.

questions.q: Which blood cells help fight germs?
questions.fact: White blood cells find and attack germs to help keep you from getting sick.

questions.q: What is the colored part of your eye called?
questions.fact: The iris is a ring of muscle that makes the pupil bigger or smaller to control light.

questions.q: How many baby teeth do most kids have?
questions.fact: Most kids have 20 baby teeth, which are later replaced by adult teeth.

questions.q: Which organs clean your blood and make urine?
questions.fact: You have two kidneys, and they filter waste out of your blood all day long.

questions.q: Which tube carries food from your mouth to your stomach?
questions.fact: Muscles in the esophagus squeeze food down to your stomach, even if you are upside down.

questions.q: Which vitamin does your skin make when sunlight hits it?
questions.fact: Vitamin D helps your body use calcium to build strong bones.

questions.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.fact: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins bring it back.

questions.q: What connects your muscles to your bones?
questions.fact: Tendons attach muscles to bones, while ligaments connect bones to other bones.

questions.q: What is the hard white outer layer of your teeth called?
questions.fact: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.

questions.q: Which bones protect your brain?
questions.fact: Your skull is made of several bones joined tightly together to guard your brain.

questions.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.fact: The heart has two upper chambers called atria and two lower chambers called ventricles.

questions.q: Which body system includes your brain, spinal cord, and nerves?
questions.fact: Your nervous system sends messages between your brain and the rest of your body.

questions.q: Where does most digestion of food happen?
questions.fact: Most food is broken down and soaked into your blood in the small intestine.

questions.q: Which protein in red blood cells carries oxygen?
questions.fact: Hemoglobin contains iron, and it is what makes blood red.

questions.q: Which ancient people built the pyramids of Giza?
questions.fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built more than 4,000 years ago as a tomb for a pharaoh.

questions.q: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.fact: George Washington became the first president in 1789.

questions.q: In what year did Christopher Columbus first reach the Americas?
questions.fact: Columbus sailed from Spain in 1492 with three ships.

questions.q: Which famous ship sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
questions.fact: The Titanic sank on its very first voyage, across the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.q: Who was the main writer of the Declaration of Independence?
questions.fact: Thomas Jefferson wrote most of the Declaration, which was adopted in 1776.

questions.q: What is the name of the long wall built across northern China?
questions.fact: The Great Wall was built and rebuilt over many centuries to protect China from invaders.

questions.q: In what year did World War II end?
questions.fact: World War II lasted from 1939 to 1945 and involved countries all over the world.

questions.q: Which famous queen of Egypt was allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony?
questions.fact: Cleopatra ruled until 30 BC. After her death, Egypt became part of the Roman Empire.

questions.q: Which Roman city was buried when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79?
questions.fact: Ash from the volcano buried Pompeii, and it stayed hidden for over 1,500 years.

questions.q: Who built a printing press with movable type in Europe around 1440?
questions.fact: Gutenberg's press made books much faster and cheaper to produce.

questions.q: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.fact: The wall split Berlin from 1961 to 1989. Germany was reunited in 1990.

questions.q: Who gave the famous "I Have a Dream" speech in 1963?
questions.fact: Martin Luther King Jr. gave the speech in Washington, D.C., calling for equal rights.

questions.q: Whose expedition was the first to sail all the way around the world?
questions.fact: Magellan died during the voyage, but his crew finished the trip around the world in 1522.

questions.q: In which country did the ancient Olympic Games begin?
questions.fact: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia, Greece, in honor of the god Zeus.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean?
questions.fact: Amelia Earhart flew alone across the Atlantic in 1932.

questions.q: Which brothers made the first powered airplane flight in 1903?
questions.fact: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew their plane at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

questions.q: What did the ancient Romans build to carry water into their cities?
questions.fact: Roman aqueducts used gentle slopes so gravity could carry water many kilometers.

questions.q: Which document, signed in 1215, limited the power of the English king?
questions.fact: King John agreed to the Magna Carta, which said even the king had to follow the law.

questions.q: What were the skilled warriors of old Japan called?
questions.fact: Samurai were Japanese warriors who followed a strict code of honor.

questions.q: Which Italian artist painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.fact: Leonardo da Vinci was also an inventor who sketched ideas for flying machines.

questions.q: What is the largest continent by area?
questions.fact: Asia is the biggest continent and covers about a third of Earth's land.

questions.q: What is the capital city of France?
questions.fact: Paris is home to the Eiffel Tower, which was finished in 1889.

questions.q: Which country is home to the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.fact: The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, off northeast Australia.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Japan?
questions.fact: Tokyo is Japan's capital. Seoul is the capital of South Korea.

questions.q: What is the tallest mountain above sea level?
questions.fact: Mount Everest is in the Himalayas, on the border of Nepal and China.

questions.q: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.fact: The Sahara covers much of North Africa and is about as big as the United States.

questions.q: Which country is shaped like a boot?
questions.fact: Italy sticks out into the Mediterranean Sea in the shape of a tall boot.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Canada?
questions.fact: Many people guess Toronto, but Ottawa is Canada's capital.

questions.q: Which river flows through London?
questions.fact: The River Thames runs through the middle of London. The Seine flows through Paris.

questions.q: What is the smallest country in the world?
questions.fact: Vatican City is a tiny country inside the city of Rome, Italy.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Australia?
questions.fact: Sydney is the biggest city, but Canberra was chosen to be Australia's capital.

questions.q: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
questions.fact: The Indian Ocean is the third largest ocean on Earth.

questions.q: What is the imaginary line around the middle of Earth called?
questions.fact: The equator divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

questions.q: Which mountain range runs down the west side of South America?
questions.fact: The Andes are the longest mountain range on land in the world.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Egypt?
questions.fact: Cairo sits beside the Nile River, not far from the pyramids of Giza.

questions.q: In which city is the Statue of Liberty?
questions.fact: France gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States, and it was dedicated in 1886.

questions.q: In which country is the ancient city of Machu Picchu?
questions.fact: Machu Picchu is an Inca city built high in the mountains of Peru.

questions.q: Which is the largest country in the world by area?
questions.fact: Russia is so wide that it stretches across two continents, Europe and Asia.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Brazil?
questions.fact: Brasilia was built from scratch and became Brazil's capital in 1960.

questions.q: Which body of water is so salty that people float easily in it?
questions.fact: The Dead Sea is so salty that fish cannot live in it, but swimmers bob like corks.

questions.q: How many players does a soccer team have on the field at once?
questions.fact: Each soccer team has 11 players on the field, including the goalkeeper.

questions.q: In which sport can a player score with a slam dunk?
questions.fact: A slam dunk is when a player jumps up and pushes the ball down through the hoop.

questions.q: How many points is a touchdown worth in American football?
questions.fact: A touchdown is worth 6 points, and the team can then try for 1 or 2 extra points.

questions.q: In tennis, what is a score of zero called?
questions.fact: In tennis, love means zero, so a score of 15 to 0 is called fifteen love.

questions.q: How often are the Summer Olympic Games usually held?
questions.fact: The Summer and Winter Olympics each happen every four years, two years apart.

questions.q: How many rings are on the Olympic flag?
questions.fact: The five linked rings stand for the parts of the world coming together at the Games.

questions.q: In baseball, how many strikes does it take to strike out?
questions.fact: Three strikes and the batter is out. Four balls let the batter walk to first base.

questions.q: How many holes are in a standard round of golf?
questions.fact: Golfers try to finish all 18 holes using as few strokes as possible.

questions.q: Which sport is played on ice with sticks and a puck?
questions.fact: A hockey puck is a hard rubber disk that can fly across the ice very fast.

questions.q: About how long is a marathon race?
questions.fact: A marathon is 42.195 kilometers, or about 26.2 miles.

questions.q: In which sport do you roll a ball to knock down ten pins?
questions.fact: Knocking down all ten pins with your first ball is called a strike.

questions.q: How many players from one team are on a basketball court at once?
questions.fact: Each basketball team has five players on the court at a time.

questions.q: In which country did the sport of judo begin?
questions.fact: Judo was created in Japan in 1882 by a teacher named Jigoro Kano.

questions.q: In soccer, which player is allowed to use their hands?
questions.fact: Only the goalkeeper may use their hands, and only inside their own penalty area.

questions.q: What is it called when one player scores three goals in one game?
questions.fact: The term hat trick started in cricket and is now used in soccer and hockey too.

questions.q: Which sport uses rackets and a feathered shuttlecock?
questions.fact: A badminton shuttlecock is also called a birdie.

questions.q: Which swimming stroke is done lying on your back?
questions.fact: Backstroke is the only Olympic swimming race that starts in the water.

questions.q: What kind of race is the Tour de France?
questions.fact: The Tour de France is a bike race that lasts about three weeks. It began in 1903.

questions.q: What do runners in a relay race pass to each other?
questions.fact: In a relay, each runner must hand the baton to the next runner inside a set zone.

questions.q: Which sport involves sliding stones across ice while teammates sweep?
questions.fact: In curling, sweeping the ice helps the stone slide farther and straighter.

questions.q: What does CPU stand for?
questions.fact: The CPU is the part of a computer that follows instructions and does calculations.

questions.q: Who received the first patent for the telephone in 1876?
questions.fact: Bell's first words on the phone were to his assistant, Mr. Watson.

questions.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
questions.fact: Tim Berners-Lee came up with the web in 1989 while working at CERN in Europe.

questions.q: What number system do computers use, made of only 0s and 1s?
questions.fact: Computers store everything, from games to photos, as long lines of 0s and 1s.

questions.q: What does GPS stand for?
questions.fact: GPS uses signals from satellites to work out exactly where you are.

questions.q: Which company makes the iPad?
questions.fact: Apple released the very first iPad in 2010.

questions.q: Which inventor created the phonograph, a machine that recorded sound?
questions.fact: Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877 and recorded himself saying a nursery rhyme.

questions.q: What does Wi-Fi let devices do?
questions.fact: Wi-Fi uses radio waves to link devices to the internet without cables.

questions.q: Which early electronic computer, finished in 1945, filled an entire room?
questions.fact: ENIAC weighed about 27 tons and used thousands of glowing vacuum tubes.

questions.q: What is a bug in computer programming?
questions.fact: Finding and fixing mistakes in code is called debugging.

questions.q: Which coding language for kids uses colorful blocks you snap together?
questions.fact: Scratch was created at MIT so anyone could learn to code by building games and stories.

questions.q: What is the name for software made to harm a computer?
questions.fact: Malware is short for malicious software. Viruses are one kind of malware.

questions.q: Which British scientist helped crack secret codes in World War II?
questions.fact: Alan Turing is often called the father of computer science.

questions.q: Who is often called the first computer programmer?
questions.fact: In the 1840s, Ada Lovelace wrote steps for a machine designed by Charles Babbage.

questions.q: What does USB stand for?
questions.fact: USB is a standard way to plug devices into computers and charge them.

questions.q: Which device turns your voice into an electrical signal?
questions.fact: A microphone changes sound into electricity. A speaker does the opposite.

questions.q: What kind of screen reacts when you tap it with your finger?
questions.fact: Touchscreens on tablets sense the tiny electric charge in your fingertip.

questions.q: What does AI stand for?
questions.fact: Artificial intelligence means computer programs that can learn and solve problems.

questions.q: Which company develops the Android operating system?
questions.fact: Android runs on phones and tablets from many different brands.

questions.q: What is HTML used to create?
questions.fact: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It tells a browser how to show a page.

questions.q: What is guacamole mainly made from?
questions.fact: Guacamole comes from Mexico and is made by mashing ripe avocados.

questions.q: Which country is famous for creating pizza?
questions.fact: Modern pizza comes from the city of Naples in Italy.

questions.q: Raisins are made by drying which fruit?
questions.fact: Raisins are grapes that have been dried. Dried plums are called prunes.

questions.q: A peanut is not a true nut. What is it?
questions.fact: Peanuts are legumes, like beans and peas, and they grow underground.

questions.q: Which country is famous for sushi?
questions.fact: Sushi is a Japanese dish made with rice flavored with vinegar, often with fish or vegetables.

questions.q: Which food is made by churning cream?
questions.fact: Shaking or stirring cream for a long time makes the fat clump together into butter.

questions.q: Popcorn is made from which grain?
questions.fact: Each popcorn kernel has a little water inside that turns to steam and makes it pop.

questions.q: Which fruit has its seeds on the outside?
questions.fact: The tiny dots on a strawberry's skin each hold a seed.

questions.q: What sweet food do bees make from flower nectar?
questions.fact: Bees store honey in wax honeycombs to feed their hive.

questions.q: Where does maple syrup come from?
questions.fact: Maple syrup is made by boiling down sap from maple trees until it gets thick and sweet.

questions.q: What is tofu made from?
questions.fact: Tofu is made by curdling soy milk and pressing it into blocks.

questions.q: Which vegetable often makes people cry when they cut it?
questions.fact: Cutting an onion releases a gas that stings your eyes and makes them water.

questions.q: Chocolate is made from the beans of which plant?
questions.fact: Cacao beans grow in pods on cacao trees and are roasted to make chocolate.

questions.q: Which spice comes from the inner bark of a tree?
questions.fact: Cinnamon bark curls up into rolls called sticks as it dries.

questions.q: Which country does the rice dish paella come from?
questions.fact: Paella comes from Valencia in Spain and is cooked in a wide, shallow pan.

questions.q: What makes bread dough rise and get fluffy?
questions.fact: Yeast is a tiny living fungus that makes gas bubbles in the dough.

questions.q: What is the main ingredient in hummus?
questions.fact: Hummus is made by blending chickpeas with sesame paste, lemon juice, and garlic.

questions.q: Which vitamin are oranges famous for?
questions.fact: Vitamin C helps your body heal cuts and fight off sickness.

questions.q: Botanists say a tomato is which part of a plant?
questions.fact: Tomatoes grow from flowers and hold seeds, so scientists call them fruits.

questions.q: Most dried pasta is made from which grain?
questions.fact: Most dried pasta is made from durum wheat flour and water.

questions.q: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.fact: The Sun is about 150 million kilometers away, much closer than any other star.

questions.q: Which star is the closest to our Sun?
questions.fact: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away, so its light takes over four years to reach us.

questions.q: What is the brightest star in the night sky?
questions.fact: Sirius is nicknamed the Dog Star because it sits in the constellation Canis Major, the Great Dog.

questions.q: Which star stays almost still in the sky above Earth's North Pole?
questions.fact: Polaris, the North Star, has helped travelers find north for hundreds of years.

questions.q: What two gases make up most of the Sun?
questions.fact: About three quarters of the Sun's mass is hydrogen.

questions.q: What process makes the Sun shine?
questions.fact: In the Sun's core, hydrogen atoms smash together to make helium and release huge amounts of energy.

questions.q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.fact: If the Sun suddenly vanished, we would not notice for about 8 minutes.

questions.q: What type of star is the Sun?
questions.fact: Even though it is called a dwarf, the Sun is bigger than most stars in the Milky Way.

questions.q: What is the visible surface of the Sun called?
questions.fact: The photosphere is about 5,500 degrees Celsius.

The air magnifies it a lot
questions.fact: If you take a photo, the Moon near the horizon is the same size as when it is high in the sky.

questions.q: What is the dusty, loose soil covering the Moon called?
questions.fact: Moon regolith is sharp and clingy because no wind or water has smoothed its grains.

questions.q: About how much Moon rock did the Apollo missions bring back to Earth?
questions.fact: Scientists are still studying these samples today.

questions.q: About how many Earths could fit inside the Sun?
questions.fact: The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth.

questions.q: About what percent of all the mass in the solar system is in the Sun?
questions.fact: All the planets, moons, asteroids and comets together make up only about 0.2 percent.

questions.q: About how hot is the center of the Sun?
questions.fact: The core is so hot and squeezed that hydrogen atoms fuse together.

questions.q: About how hot is the surface of the Sun?
questions.fact: That is hot enough to melt and boil any metal on Earth.

questions.q: About how many times wider is the Sun than Earth?
questions.fact: If the Sun were as tall as a front door, Earth would be about the size of a nickel.

questions.q: What is the roughly 11-year rise and fall in sunspots called?
questions.fact: At the peak of the solar cycle, there are more sunspots, solar flares and bright auroras.

questions.q: What is a solar flare?
choices: A ring of light around the Sun
A sudden burst of energy from the Sun
questions.fact: Big solar flares can disrupt radio signals and GPS on Earth.

questions.q: Which NASA spacecraft has flown closer to the Sun than any other?
questions.fact: In December 2024, Parker Solar Probe passed about 6.1 million kilometers from the Sun's surface.

questions.q: Which part of the Sun makes its energy?
questions.fact: Energy made in the core can take thousands of years or more to work its way out to the surface.

questions.q: Why should you never look straight at the Sun, even during a partial eclipse?
choices: It can permanently damage your eyes
questions.fact: Special eclipse glasses block almost all of the Sun's light so you can watch safely.

questions.q: What is the dark center of a shadow during an eclipse called?
questions.fact: The lighter outer part of the shadow is called the penumbra.

questions.q: On what date in 2024 did a total solar eclipse cross Mexico, the United States and Canada?
questions.fact: Millions of people watched as the Moon covered the Sun for up to about four minutes.

questions.q: What is an annular solar eclipse?
choices: When the Moon covers the Sun's middle but leaves a ring of light
When two moons cover the Sun
questions.fact: It happens when the Moon is a bit farther from Earth and looks too small to cover the Sun completely.

questions.q: What is the harvest moon?
choices: The full moon closest to the start of autumn
The last moon of the year
questions.fact: Long ago, its bright light helped farmers keep harvesting crops after sunset.

questions.q: About how long is one full day, from sunrise to sunrise, on the Moon?
questions.fact: So any spot on the Moon gets about two weeks of daylight followed by about two weeks of night.

questions.q: Why do temperatures on the Moon swing from very hot to very cold?
choices: It has no atmosphere to hold heat in
It is very close to the Sun
questions.fact: The Moon's surface can go from about 120 degrees Celsius in daylight to below minus 170 at night.

questions.q: How wide is the Moon compared to Earth?
questions.fact: The Moon is about 3,474 kilometers across.

questions.q: Where does Earth's Moon rank in size among all the moons in the solar system?
questions.fact: Only Ganymede, Titan, Callisto and Io are bigger.

questions.q: What are the bright streaks that spread out from some craters on the Moon called?
questions.fact: The crater Tycho has rays that stretch across much of the Moon.

questions.q: Which moon is slowly spiraling toward its planet and may break apart someday?
questions.fact: Mars's moon Phobos gets about 2 meters closer to Mars every 100 years.

questions.q: Which planet is often called Earth's twin because it is almost the same size?
questions.fact: Venus is about 95 percent as wide as Earth, but it is nothing like Earth on the surface.

questions.q: What are the clouds of Venus made of?
questions.fact: The thick clouds reflect so much sunlight that they make Venus shine brightly in our sky.

questions.q: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun?
questions.fact: Venus has a runaway greenhouse effect that keeps it at about 465 degrees Celsius day and night.

questions.q: About how hot is the surface of Venus?
questions.fact: That is hot enough to melt lead.

questions.q: The air pressure on Venus's surface is like being how deep in Earth's ocean?
questions.fact: The air on Venus is more than 90 times heavier than on Earth.

questions.q: Which Soviet spacecraft series sent back the first pictures from the surface of Venus?
questions.fact: Venera landers only lasted a short time before the heat and pressure destroyed them.

questions.q: Most features on Venus are named after whom?
questions.fact: Its tallest mountains, Maxwell Montes, are the main exception.

questions.q: Craters on Mercury are named after what kind of people?
questions.fact: Mercury has craters named after Beethoven and Mark Twain.

questions.q: What has been found in shadowy craters at Mercury's poles, even though Mercury is close to the Sun?
questions.fact: Sunlight never reaches the floors of these deep polar craters, so the ice never melts.

questions.q: Which spacecraft orbited Mercury from 2011 to 2015?
questions.fact: MESSENGER found evidence of water ice in Mercury's polar craters.

questions.q: What gas makes up most of Mars's thin atmosphere?
questions.fact: The air on Mars is about 100 times thinner than on Earth.

questions.q: What color are sunsets on Mars?
questions.fact: Fine dust in the Martian air scatters blue light near the Sun at sunset.

questions.q: What are Mars's polar ice caps made of?
choices: Water ice and frozen carbon dioxide
questions.fact: Frozen carbon dioxide is also called dry ice.

questions.q: How wide is Mars compared to Earth?
questions.fact: Mars is the second smallest planet after Mercury.

questions.q: Why does Mars sometimes seem to move backward across our sky?
choices: Earth is passing it as they both orbit
questions.fact: This is called retrograde motion, and it puzzled ancient astronomers.

questions.q: What was the famous Face on Mars photographed in 1976?
choices: A hill that looked like a face because of shadows
questions.fact: Later sharper photos showed it was just an ordinary mesa.

questions.q: Which spacecraft was the first to orbit Mars, in 1971?
questions.fact: Mariner 9 arrived during a planet-wide dust storm and had to wait for it to clear.

questions.q: In what year did NASA's Viking 1 land on Mars?
questions.fact: The Viking landers carried experiments to look for signs of life in the soil.

questions.q: Which NASA lander dug up water ice near Mars's north pole in 2008?
questions.fact: Phoenix scraped the soil and watched small chunks of ice slowly disappear.

questions.q: What did NASA's InSight lander mostly study?
choices: Marsquakes and the inside of Mars
questions.fact: InSight recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes.

questions.q: What is the name of the crater where the Perseverance rover landed?
questions.fact: Jezero Crater once held a lake, which makes it a good place to look for signs of ancient life.

questions.q: Which country reached Mars orbit on its very first try in 2014?
questions.fact: India's Mangalyaan mission cost less than many Hollywood space movies.

questions.q: What is the name of China's first Mars rover, which landed in 2021?
questions.fact: Zhurong is named after a fire god from Chinese myths.

questions.q: What are China's Chang'e Moon missions named after?
choices: A Moon goddess from Chinese legend
questions.fact: In the legend, Chang'e lives on the Moon with a jade rabbit, and China's Moon rovers are named Yutu, meaning jade rabbit.

questions.q: Who was China's first astronaut, in 2003?
questions.fact: China became the third country to launch a person into space on its own rocket.

questions.q: What are Russian astronauts called?
questions.fact: The word cosmonaut comes from Greek words meaning universe sailor.

questions.q: What does the word astronaut mean in Greek?
questions.fact: Astro means star and naut means sailor.

questions.q: Who was the commander of Apollo 13?
questions.fact: The story of Apollo 13 was made into a famous movie in 1995.

questions.q: What did the Apollo 13 crew radio to Mission Control after the explosion?
questions.fact: People often misquote it as Houston, we have a problem.

questions.q: What did Neil Armstrong say as he stepped onto the Moon?
choices: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind
questions.fact: About 600 million people watched the landing on TV.

questions.q: What words are on the plaque left on the Moon by Apollo 11?
choices: We came in peace for all mankind
questions.fact: The plaque is attached to the leg of the lunar module's base, which stayed on the Moon.

questions.q: Which US president challenged America to land a person on the Moon before 1970?
questions.fact: He made the challenge in a speech to Congress in 1961.

questions.q: Which two countries competed in the Space Race?
questions.fact: The Space Race lasted from the late 1950s to the early 1970s.

questions.q: What were NASA's first seven astronauts called?
questions.fact: They were chosen in 1959 from a group of military test pilots.

questions.q: How many astronauts flew in each Gemini spacecraft?
questions.fact: Gemini is Latin for twins, a good name for a two-person spacecraft.

questions.q: How many astronauts flew on each Apollo Moon mission?
questions.fact: Two astronauts landed on the Moon while the third stayed in orbit.

questions.q: Which astronaut flew to space again in 1998 at the age of 77?
questions.fact: John Glenn had first orbited Earth 36 years earlier.

questions.q: Who was the first African American woman to travel to space?
questions.fact: Mae Jemison flew on the Space Shuttle Endeavour in 1992.

questions.q: Which NASA mathematician checked the orbit math for John Glenn's flight and was featured in the movie Hidden Figures?
questions.fact: John Glenn asked for her to check the computer's numbers before he would fly.

questions.q: Who led the team that wrote the software for the Apollo guidance computer?
questions.fact: A famous photo shows her standing next to a stack of code printouts as tall as she was.

questions.q: Which astronaut recorded a music video of the song Space Oddity on the International Space Station in 2013?
questions.fact: It was the first music video filmed in space.

questions.q: Which astronaut spent almost a year on the International Space Station while an identical twin stayed on Earth for a NASA study?
questions.fact: The study compared the twins to learn how long spaceflight changes the human body.

questions.q: Who holds the record for the longest single trip in space, as of 2025?
questions.fact: Valeri Polyakov spent about 437 days in a row on the Mir space station in the 1990s.

questions.q: Which American astronaut has spent the most total days in space, as of 2025?
questions.fact: As of 2025, Peggy Whitson has spent close to 700 days in space over several missions.

questions.q: Who wrote and hosted the famous 1980 TV series Cosmos?
questions.fact: Carl Sagan also helped choose what went on the Voyager golden records.

questions.q: Which scientist studied black holes and wrote the book A Brief History of Time?
questions.fact: Stephen Hawking predicted that black holes slowly give off a faint glow, now called Hawking radiation.

questions.q: Who is the Hubble Space Telescope named after?
questions.fact: Edwin Hubble proved that many fuzzy patches in the sky are whole other galaxies.

questions.q: What problem did the Hubble Space Telescope have right after launch?
choices: Its main mirror was slightly the wrong shape
It was in the wrong orbit
questions.fact: Astronauts fixed it in 1993 by adding corrective optics, like giving Hubble glasses.

questions.q: How many times did astronauts fly to the Hubble Space Telescope to fix and upgrade it?
questions.fact: The last servicing mission was in 2009.

questions.q: What did Hubble's famous Pillars of Creation picture show?
choices: Towers of gas and dust where stars are forming
questions.fact: The pillars are in the Eagle Nebula, about 6,500 light-years away.

questions.q: What did the Hubble Deep Field picture reveal in a tiny dark patch of sky?
questions.fact: Almost every speck of light in the picture is a whole galaxy, not a single star.

questions.q: Which NASA space telescope studies X-rays from very hot things like exploding stars?
questions.fact: X-rays from space are blocked by Earth's air, so X-ray telescopes must be in orbit.

questions.q: Which giant radio telescope in Puerto Rico collapsed in 2020?
questions.fact: Arecibo appeared in movies, including the James Bond film GoldenEye.

questions.q: Which country built FAST, the giant 500-meter-wide radio telescope?
questions.fact: FAST sits in a natural bowl-shaped valley.

questions.q: What do radio telescopes detect?
questions.fact: Radio telescopes can work during the day and even through clouds.

questions.q: Why are many big telescopes built on tall mountains?
choices: It is cheaper to build there
There is less air and cloud to blur the view
questions.fact: Many of the world's best telescopes sit high on mountains in Hawaii and Chile.

questions.q: What is a galaxy?
choices: A huge group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity
questions.fact: Scientists estimate there are hundreds of billions of galaxies in the universe we can observe.

questions.q: About how many stars are in the Milky Way?
questions.fact: Most of these stars are too faint to see without a telescope.

questions.q: Which type of galaxy looks like a round or oval ball of stars?
questions.fact: Elliptical galaxies usually have older stars and little gas for making new ones.

questions.q: What are the two small galaxies, seen from the Southern Hemisphere, that are close neighbors of the Milky Way?
questions.fact: They are named after explorer Ferdinand Magellan, whose crew described them.

questions.q: What is dark matter?
choices: Unseen matter that scientists detect only by its gravity
questions.fact: Scientists think there is about five times more dark matter than regular matter.

questions.q: What is a quasar?
choices: The super bright center of a faraway galaxy powered by a black hole
questions.fact: Some quasars shine brighter than a trillion Suns.

questions.q: What is a white dwarf?
choices: The small, hot leftover core of a star like the Sun
questions.fact: A white dwarf is about the size of Earth but has about as much mass as the Sun.

questions.q: What is a brown dwarf?
choices: An object too big to be a planet but too small to be a true star
questions.fact: Brown dwarfs never got hot enough to fuse hydrogen like real stars.

questions.q: What is a neutron star?
choices: The super-dense core left behind after some supernovas
questions.fact: A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.

questions.q: What makes stars seem to twinkle?
questions.fact: Seen from space, stars do not twinkle at all.

questions.q: What happens to the light from a galaxy that is moving away from us?
questions.fact: This is called redshift, and it helps scientists measure how fast galaxies are moving.

questions.q: What is the faint glow left over from the Big Bang called?
questions.fact: It was discovered by accident in 1965 by two scientists who first thought the signal came from pigeon droppings on their antenna.

questions.q: What did the LIGO detectors observe for the first time in 2015?
questions.fact: The waves came from two black holes crashing together more than a billion light-years away.

questions.q: About how cold is deep space, far from any star?
questions.fact: That is only a few degrees above absolute zero, the coldest temperature possible.

questions.q: Which planet is fifth from the Sun?
questions.fact: Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt.

questions.q: Which planet lies between Saturn and Neptune?
questions.fact: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun.

questions.q: Which is the largest of the four rocky planets?
questions.fact: The rocky planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.

questions.q: What kind of planets are Jupiter and Saturn?
questions.fact: They are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, like the Sun.

questions.q: What are Uranus and Neptune often called?
questions.fact: They contain lots of water, ammonia and methane, which scientists call ices.

questions.q: What would happen if a spacecraft tried to land on Jupiter?
choices: There is no solid surface to land on
questions.fact: The gas just gets thicker and hotter the deeper you go, until it would crush any spacecraft.

questions.q: About how many times wider is Jupiter than Earth?
questions.fact: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

questions.q: What is the main gas in Jupiter's atmosphere?
questions.fact: Jupiter is about 90 percent hydrogen by number of molecules.

questions.q: What has been happening to Jupiter's Great Red Spot over the last hundred years?
choices: It moved to the north pole
questions.fact: Even though it has shrunk, the Great Red Spot is still wider than Earth.

questions.q: What was the Great Dark Spot seen by Voyager 2 in 1989?
questions.fact: When Hubble looked at Neptune a few years later, the spot had disappeared.

questions.q: Many of the moons of Uranus are named after characters from which writer's plays?
questions.fact: Uranus has moons named Miranda, Titania, Oberon and Juliet.

questions.q: Which planet is named after the Roman god of war?
questions.fact: Mars's red color reminded ancient people of blood and battle.

questions.q: Which planet is named after the fast messenger of the Roman gods?
questions.fact: The name fits, because Mercury is the fastest-moving planet.

questions.q: Which planet is named after the Roman goddess of love and beauty?
questions.fact: Venus is the only planet named after a female god.

questions.q: Which planet is named after the king of the Roman gods?
questions.fact: It is a good name for the biggest planet in the solar system.

questions.q: Which planet is named after the Roman god of the sea?
questions.fact: Its deep blue color makes the name fit well.

questions.q: Which planet is named after an ancient Greek god of the sky?
questions.fact: Uranus is the only planet named after a Greek god instead of a Roman one.

questions.q: Which planet is named after the Roman god of farming?
questions.fact: Saturday is also named after Saturn.

questions.q: Which is the widest dwarf planet?
questions.fact: Eris is a little smaller than Pluto but has a bit more mass.

questions.q: How many dwarf planets are officially recognized, as of 2025?
questions.fact: As of 2025, they are Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

questions.q: Which dwarf planet is stretched into an egg shape because it spins so fast?
questions.fact: Haumea spins once about every four hours, one of the fastest spins of any big object in the solar system.

questions.q: Which NASA spacecraft visited both the asteroid Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres?
questions.fact: Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth.

questions.q: Which NASA mission brought back a sample from the asteroid Bennu in 2023?
questions.fact: The sample capsule parachuted down into the Utah desert.

questions.q: What did NASA's DART spacecraft do in 2022?
choices: Crashed into an asteroid to change its path
questions.fact: DART hit the small asteroid Dimorphos and successfully shortened its orbit.

questions.q: Which Japanese spacecraft brought back samples from the asteroid Ryugu?
questions.fact: Hayabusa means peregrine falcon in Japanese.

questions.q: Which asteroid will pass very close to Earth, even closer than some satellites, in April 2029?
questions.fact: Scientists have checked carefully, and Apophis will not hit Earth in 2029.

questions.q: What flattened about 80 million trees in Siberia in 1908?
choices: A space rock exploding in the air
questions.fact: This is called the Tunguska event, and the blast happened above the ground.

questions.q: In which country did a meteor explode over the city of Chelyabinsk in 2013?
questions.fact: The blast shattered windows across the city, and many people caught it on dashboard cameras.

questions.q: In which country is the Hoba meteorite, the largest single meteorite ever found?
questions.fact: The Hoba meteorite weighs about 60 tons and was never moved from where it landed.

questions.q: In which US state is the famous Meteor Crater?
questions.fact: Meteor Crater is about 1.2 kilometers wide and was made about 50,000 years ago.

questions.q: Why do scientists search for meteorites in Antarctica?
choices: Dark rocks are easy to spot on the white ice
It is warmer than other places
questions.fact: Moving ice also carries meteorites to certain spots, piling them up.

questions.q: Have meteorites from Mars been found on Earth?
choices: Yes, they were blasted off Mars by impacts
questions.fact: Scientists can tell they are from Mars because gas trapped inside matches the Martian air.

questions.q: Which comet was easy to see without a telescope for months in 1997?
questions.fact: Hale-Bopp was visible to the naked eye for about 18 months.

questions.q: Which comet broke into pieces and crashed into Jupiter in 1994?
questions.fact: Some of the impact scars on Jupiter were bigger than Earth.

questions.q: What are space junk and space debris?
choices: Old satellites and broken pieces orbiting Earth
questions.fact: Even a tiny paint chip can be dangerous because it moves faster than a bullet.

questions.q: What is special about a satellite in geostationary orbit?
choices: It stays above the same spot on Earth
questions.fact: Geostationary satellites orbit about 36,000 kilometers above the equator.

questions.q: About how fast must something go to escape Earth's gravity completely?
questions.fact: This speed is called escape velocity.

questions.q: About how high above Earth does space begin, by the most common definition?
questions.fact: This boundary is called the Karman line.

questions.q: What is the floating, weightless feeling that astronauts have in orbit called?
questions.fact: In microgravity, astronauts can push off a wall with one finger and float across a room.

questions.q: Why do astronauts on the International Space Station exercise about two hours a day?
choices: To keep their bones and muscles strong
questions.fact: Without gravity to push against, bones and muscles get weaker quickly.

questions.q: What happens to astronauts' height while they live in space?
questions.fact: Without gravity squeezing their spines, astronauts can grow a few centimeters taller, but it goes away back on Earth.

questions.q: How do astronauts sleep on the International Space Station?
choices: In sleeping bags attached to the wall
questions.fact: In microgravity there is no up or down, so sleeping on a wall feels the same as on a floor.

questions.q: What do astronauts often eat instead of bread, so crumbs do not float into equipment?
questions.fact: Floating crumbs could get into astronauts' eyes or clog machines.

questions.q: What does the International Space Station recycle into clean drinking water?
questions.fact: The station's system recycles about 98 percent of the water on board.

questions.q: What shape does a candle flame take in microgravity?
questions.fact: Without gravity, hot air does not rise, so the flame spreads out evenly in all directions.

questions.q: Why are spacesuits usually white?
choices: So they glow in the dark
To reflect sunlight and stay cooler
questions.fact: In direct sunlight in space, a dark suit would soak up too much heat.

questions.q: What is a spacewalk officially called?
questions.fact: Astronauts on spacewalks are tied to the station with safety tethers.

questions.q: What keeps a spacecraft from burning up when it comes back into Earth's air?
questions.fact: Reentry heats the outside of a capsule to well over 1,000 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What were the first animals sent into space, in 1947?
questions.fact: The fruit flies rode on a V-2 rocket and came back alive.

questions.q: What was the name of the first chimpanzee to fly into space, in 1961?
questions.fact: Ham was trained to pull levers during the flight, proving that tasks could be done in space.

questions.q: What were the dogs Belka and Strelka famous for in 1960?
choices: Being the first dogs to orbit Earth and come back alive
Pulling a sled to the South Pole
questions.fact: One of Strelka's puppies was given as a gift to US President John F. Kennedy's family.

questions.q: What is the 1990 photo of Earth taken by Voyager 1 from about 6 billion kilometers away called?
questions.fact: In it, Earth is a tiny speck less than a pixel wide.

questions.q: What is the famous 1972 photo of the whole Earth, taken by the Apollo 17 crew, called?
questions.fact: It is one of the most shared photographs ever taken.

questions.q: How do scientists find many planets around other stars?
choices: By watching for stars to dim slightly when a planet passes in front
questions.fact: This is called the transit method, and the Kepler telescope used it to find thousands of planets.

questions.q: What is the habitable zone around a star?
choices: The area where it is the right temperature for liquid water
The part of a planet with cities
questions.fact: It is also nicknamed the Goldilocks zone, not too hot and not too cold.

questions.q: Which star system, announced in 2017, has seven Earth-sized planets?
questions.fact: Three of TRAPPIST-1's planets are in the zone where liquid water might exist.

questions.q: What is the line between day and night on a planet or moon called?
questions.fact: Craters near the terminator cast long shadows, so it is the best place to look at the Moon with a telescope.

questions.q: What is the point in the sky directly above your head called?
questions.fact: The point directly below you, through the Earth, is called the nadir.

questions.q: How much is Earth's axis tilted?
questions.fact: This tilt is the reason Earth has seasons.

questions.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
questions.fact: When your half of Earth tilts toward the Sun, sunlight hits more directly and it is summer.

questions.q: During which month is Earth closest to the Sun?
questions.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during winter in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: What is the day with the most hours of daylight in the year called?
questions.fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, it usually falls on June 20 or 21.

questions.q: What is special about an equinox?
choices: Day and night are about the same length everywhere
questions.fact: Equinox comes from Latin words meaning equal night.

questions.q: On average, which planet is closest to Earth?
questions.fact: Venus comes closest at times, but Mercury stays nearer on average because it never strays far from the Sun.

questions.q: Can the Great Wall of China be seen with the naked eye from the Moon?
questions.fact: The wall is very long but narrow, and from the Moon even whole continents look small.

questions.q: Which space agency is called ESA?
questions.fact: ESA has more than 20 member countries.

questions.q: What is India's space agency called?
questions.fact: ISRO stands for Indian Space Research Organisation.

questions.q: What is Japan's space agency called?
questions.fact: JAXA stands for Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency.

questions.q: Which NASA center in Florida launches many rockets?
questions.fact: Apollo 11 launched from Kennedy Space Center in 1969.

questions.q: Which NASA center in Houston runs Mission Control for astronaut flights?
questions.fact: When astronauts radio Houston, they are talking to Mission Control there.

questions.q: What is the zone of orbits up to about 2,000 kilometers above Earth called?
questions.fact: Most satellites, and every human spaceflight except Apollo, have stayed in low Earth orbit.

questions.q: What was the name of the world's first space station, launched in 1971?
questions.fact: Salyut 1 was launched by the Soviet Union.

questions.q: Who became the first emperor of Rome?
questions.fact: Augustus, who was born with the name Octavian, became Rome's first emperor in 27 BC.

questions.q: Which wonder of the ancient world was a giant lighthouse in Egypt?
questions.fact: The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood on the island of Pharos and was one of the tallest buildings of the ancient world.

questions.q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is the only one still standing?
questions.fact: The Great Pyramid was built about 4,500 years ago for the pharaoh Khufu.

questions.q: What were the picture symbols used for writing in ancient Egypt called?
questions.fact: Hieroglyphs could be written left to right, right to left, or top to bottom.

questions.q: Which stone helped experts finally read Egyptian hieroglyphs?
questions.fact: The Rosetta Stone has the same message in three scripts, which helped Jean-François Champollion crack hieroglyphs in 1822.

questions.q: Which young pharaoh's tomb was found almost untouched in 1922?
questions.fact: Howard Carter found King Tut's tomb in the Valley of the Kings, packed with golden treasures.

questions.q: What wedge-shaped writing was invented in ancient Mesopotamia?
questions.fact: Cuneiform was pressed into wet clay tablets with the end of a cut reed.

questions.q: Which river did farming in ancient Egypt depend on?
questions.fact: The Nile flooded every year and left rich black soil behind for growing crops.

questions.q: Which Greek city-state was famous for its tough warriors?
questions.fact: Spartan boys started their military training at about age 7.

questions.q: In which ancient Greek city did democracy first develop?
questions.fact: Athenian democracy began around 508 BC, but only free adult men were allowed to vote.

questions.q: Which Macedonian king built a huge empire before he died at age 32?
questions.fact: Alexander's empire stretched from Greece all the way to the edge of India.

questions.q: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with war elephants to attack Rome?
questions.fact: Hannibal crossed the Alps in 218 BC, and many of his elephants did not survive the cold.

questions.q: What were the fighters who battled to entertain crowds in Roman arenas called?
questions.fact: Many gladiators were enslaved people or prisoners, but the best ones became as famous as sports stars.

questions.q: What is the name of the giant ancient arena in the middle of Rome?
questions.fact: The Colosseum was finished in AD 80 and could hold around 50,000 people.

questions.q: Which Roman leader was killed on the Ides of March in 44 BC?
questions.fact: The Ides of March is another name for March 15.

questions.q: What language did the ancient Romans speak?
questions.fact: Latin is the root of Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian.

questions.q: According to legend, which city was captured by soldiers hiding inside a wooden horse?
questions.fact: The story of the Trojan Horse comes from ancient Greek myths and poems.

questions.q: Who led the Huns in their attacks on the Roman Empire?
questions.fact: Attila was so feared that Romans called him the Scourge of God.

questions.q: Which Mongol leader founded the Mongol Empire in 1206?
questions.fact: At its biggest, the Mongol Empire was the largest connected land empire in history.

questions.q: Which grandson of Genghis Khan started the Yuan dynasty in China?
questions.fact: The traveler Marco Polo wrote about visiting the court of Kublai Khan.

questions.q: Which Italian traveler wrote about his journey to China in the 1200s?
questions.fact: Marco Polo said he spent about 17 years in China working for Kublai Khan.
